courseTitle: How IT Teams Work: Agile, Waterfall, Scrum, Kanban & Software Releases

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one real small-business idea (a bakery's online ordering page, a gym's class-booking app, anything concrete). Sketch a one-page delivery plan for it twice: once as a Waterfall project with the 6 phases (Requirements, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, Maintenance) each given a fixed duration, and once as an Agile plan broken into three 1-week sprints with a one-sentence goal per sprint. Write 2-3 sentences explaining which model you'd actually recommend for this specific project and why.
slots.deliverable: A one-page written comparison showing the same project planned under Waterfall's 6 phases and under 3 Agile sprints, plus a short recommendation with reasoning.

slots.practicalActivity: For the same project idea from the last session, write 4 user stories in the "As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]" shape, each with at least 2 specific, checkable acceptance criteria (not vague ones like "it works"). Then assign the three Scrum roles (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers) to yourself and two imaginary teammates, and write a 3-sentence Sprint Planning summary stating the sprint goal and which of your 4 stories you'd pull into a one-week sprint.
slots.deliverable: 4 written user stories with acceptance criteria, plus a short Sprint Planning summary naming the sprint goal and the stories committed to it.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a real Kanban board for your project's 4 user stories, either on paper, in a spreadsheet, or in a free tool (Trello, GitHub Projects, or Jira's free tier) with columns Backlog, To Do, In Progress, Review, Done. Break each story into 2-3 smaller task cards (8-12 cards total), set a WIP limit of 3 on "In Progress," and move at least 3 cards through two columns to simulate a day of work. Mark one card "Blocked" with a one-sentence reason.
slots.deliverable: A working Kanban board (screenshot or photo) with at least 8 task cards distributed across its columns, a visible WIP limit on In Progress, and one card marked Blocked with a stated reason.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one of your user stories and write a short narrative tracing it through Dev, QA, UAT, and Production exactly as the lesson's ticket-journey diagram lays it out: who picks it up, what a code review would check, what a QA test plan would verify (including one edge case), what the business stakeholder would check in UAT, and what "deployed" means for this specific story. Then write one sentence for each environment naming the specific question it answers.
slots.deliverable: A written walkthrough of one user story through all 4 environments (Dev, QA, UAT, Production), with the owner and the specific question answered at each stage.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Git if needed, run git init to create a real local repository for your project, add a .gitignore, and make 3 real commits with specific messages (not "fixed stuff") as you add a README and two placeholder files representing your user stories. Create a branch named add-user-stories, commit on it, then merge it back. If you have a GitHub account, push the repo and open a pull request for the branch before merging it there instead.
slots.deliverable: A real local (or GitHub) Git repository with a .gitignore, at least 3 commits with specific messages, and one branch that was created, committed to, and merged.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a release checklist for shipping your project's first feature, covering all four required items: Approval (who signs off), Monitoring (what you'd watch after release), Rollback plan (the specific way to undo it), and Release notes (a real, specific note like the lesson's example, not "various improvements"). Then pick one deployment strategy (blue-green, canary, rolling, or feature flag) that fits this release and write 2-3 sentences justifying the choice over the other three.
slots.deliverable: A written release checklist (approval, monitoring, rollback plan, release notes) for one feature, plus a justified choice of deployment strategy.

slots.practicalActivity: Work through the full Castlebridge Retail capstone scenario from the lesson: write 3+ user stories (revenue-by-region, revenue-by-category, automatic refresh) with acceptance criteria, build a 5-column Kanban board and place the stories on it, write a short QA test plan including the zero-sales edge case, write a one-paragraph UAT sign-off in the sales director's voice, write a specific release note, and write how you'd investigate and communicate about the simulated production incident where a region shows zero sales two days after launch.
slots.deliverable: A complete capstone packet: 3+ user stories with acceptance criteria, a Kanban board, a QA test plan with an edge case, a UAT sign-off, release notes, and a written incident-response plan for the zero-sales scenario.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: A student finishing this course can read and participate in any IT team's actual workflow on day one — writing real user stories, working a Kanban board, understanding why a change passes through Dev/QA/UAT/Production, using Git's clone-branch-commit-push-PR cycle, and reasoning about a CI/CD release and rollback plan.
